title: Recent Developments in 3D Computer Vision
blurb: The last lecture: deep networks inside the SLAM pipeline (D3VO), NeRF versus Gaussian splatting, single-view density fields and scene completion, reconstruction from casual video, and event cameras. No past-exam questions exist for this chapter yet — everything here is derived from the SS26 slides.

knowledge_points.title: Deep Networks inside the SLAM Pipeline
knowledge_points.recap:
**The idea.** Rather than replacing geometry with a network, modern systems keep the classical front-end/back-end structure and let a network supply the quantities that are hard to obtain geometrically — in particular **depth from a single image**, which resolves the scale ambiguity of monocular vision, and a **prior on the pose**.
**D3VO (Yang et al., CVPR 2020)** predicts three things and feeds them into a direct visual-odometry system:
$\bullet$ **Deep depth** $D_t$ — a monocular depth map, giving metric scale that monocular VO cannot recover on its own;
$\bullet$ **Deep pose** $T_{t't}$ — a relative-pose prior used to initialise tracking;
$\bullet$ **Deep uncertainty** $\Sigma_t$ — a per-pixel confidence, which weights the photometric residuals so that unreliable pixels (moving objects, reflections, over-exposure) contribute less.
**Self-supervised training.** No ground-truth depth is needed. The networks are trained by **view synthesis**: warp frame $t'$ into frame $t$ using the predicted depth and pose, and penalise the photometric difference,
$$L_{\text{self}}=r\big(I_t,\ I_{t'\to t}\big).$$
This is exactly the brightness-constancy residual of Chapters 4 and 7, now used as a **training loss** instead of an optimisation objective.
**Deep affine brightness correction.** Real video has changing exposure, so the network also predicts per-frame affine parameters $a_t^{t'},b_t^{t'}$ and the loss becomes $r\big(a_t^{t'}I_t+b_t^{t'},\ I_{t'\to t}\big)$ — the learned counterpart of DSO's photometric model (irradiance rather than brightness constancy).
**Uncertainty in the loss.** With a predicted variance the residual is weighted and regularised,
$$L=\frac{r(\cdot)}{\Sigma_t}+\log\Sigma_t,$$
the standard heteroscedastic (aleatoric) uncertainty formulation: the $1/\Sigma$ down-weights hard pixels while $\log\Sigma$ prevents the network from declaring everything uncertain.
**Result.** On KITTI and EuRoC, deep-augmented VO closes much of the gap to stereo systems while remaining monocular — the practical message of the chapter is *hybrid*, not *end-to-end*.

questions.q: Describe how D3VO integrates deep networks into a direct visual-odometry system: what does it predict, how is it trained, and why is each predicted quantity useful?
questions.answer:
**What it predicts.** A **DepthNet** produces a monocular depth map $D_t$ and a **PoseNet** a relative pose $T_{t't}$; in addition the network outputs a per-pixel **uncertainty** $\Sigma_t$ and per-frame **affine brightness** parameters $a_t^{t'},b_t^{t'}$. These feed a classical front-end tracking / back-end optimisation pipeline.
**How it is trained — self-supervised view synthesis.** No ground-truth depth is required: frame $t'$ is warped into frame $t$ using the predicted depth and pose, and the loss is the photometric residual
$$L_{\text{self}}=r\big(a_t^{t'}I_t+b_t^{t'},\ I_{t'\to t}\big).$$
With uncertainty this becomes $\dfrac{r(\cdot)}{\Sigma_t}+\log\Sigma_t$.
**Why each is useful.** **Depth** supplies the **metric scale** that a monocular system cannot observe, and initialises the inverse-depth of new points. **Pose** gives a good initialisation for the highly non-convex photometric alignment, enlarging its basin of convergence. **Uncertainty** re-weights the residuals so that moving objects, specularities and over-exposed regions contribute less. **Affine brightness** absorbs exposure changes that would otherwise violate brightness constancy.
questions.extend: The loss is the same photometric residual as in direct SLAM — used at training time instead of test time. Geometry is not replaced, it is *initialised and weighted* by learning.

knowledge_points.title: NeRF versus Gaussian Splatting
knowledge_points.recap:
**Neural Radiance Fields (Mildenhall et al., ECCV 2020).** The scene is stored **implicitly** in the weights of an MLP
$$F_\Theta:(x,y,z,\theta,\phi)\ \longmapsto\ (\text{colour }c,\ \text{density }\sigma),$$
mapping a 3D position and viewing direction to colour and volume density (the view direction is what lets it model specularities). A pixel is rendered by **volume rendering** along its ray: sample points, accumulate colour weighted by density and transmittance. Training minimises the photometric difference between rendered and observed images over a set of posed images — again a photometric residual, exactly as in Chapters 4, 7 and 9.
**3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., SIGGRAPH 2023).** The scene is stored **explicitly** as a large set of 3D Gaussians, each with a mean, an anisotropic covariance, an opacity and view-dependent colour (spherical harmonics). Rendering **splats** each Gaussian into the image (Westover's 1991 idea) and $\alpha$-blends them front to back — a rasterisation, not a ray march.
**The trade-off.**
$\bullet$ **Speed.** Splatting rasterises and is **real-time** (hundreds of fps); NeRF must evaluate an MLP at many samples per ray, so it is orders of magnitude slower without heavy acceleration structures.
$\bullet$ **Training time.** Minutes for splatting versus hours for a vanilla NeRF.
$\bullet$ **Representation.** Implicit and continuous (NeRF) versus explicit primitives (splatting) — the same explicit/implicit trade-off as meshes versus level sets in Chapter 8. Explicit primitives are easy to edit and prune; an implicit field is compact and naturally handles arbitrary topology.
$\bullet$ **Memory.** NeRF stores a network of a few MB; splatting stores millions of Gaussians, typically hundreds of MB.
$\bullet$ **Quality.** Comparable on standard novel-view-synthesis benchmarks; splatting is sharper on textured detail, NeRF-style fields degrade more gracefully in poorly observed regions.
**Common ground.** Both are **novel-view-synthesis** methods trained by photometric reconstruction from posed images — they need camera poses (usually from COLMAP) and they optimise appearance, not an explicit surface. Extracting a clean mesh from either requires a further step.

questions.q: Compare Neural Radiance Fields and 3D Gaussian Splatting: what does each store, how is each rendered, and what are the practical trade-offs?
questions.answer:
**NeRF — implicit.** The scene lives in the weights of an MLP $F_\Theta:(x,y,z,\theta,\phi)\mapsto(c,\sigma)$ mapping a 3D position and viewing direction to colour and volume density. Rendering is **volume rendering**: sample points along each camera ray and accumulate colour weighted by density and transmittance.
**Gaussian splatting — explicit.** The scene is a set of millions of 3D Gaussians, each with a mean, an anisotropic covariance, an opacity and view-dependent colour. Rendering **splats** (projects) each Gaussian into the image and $\alpha$-blends them front to back — a rasterisation.
**Trade-offs.** Splatting renders in **real time** and trains in minutes, whereas a vanilla NeRF needs many network evaluations per ray and hours of training. NeRF is compact (a few MB of weights) and continuous; splatting needs hundreds of MB but is directly editable and prunable. Quality is broadly comparable on novel-view synthesis, with splatting sharper on fine texture.
**What they share.** Both are trained by **photometric** reconstruction from a set of **posed** images (typically posed by classical SfM), both target novel-view synthesis rather than an explicit surface, and both need an extra step to extract a mesh.
questions.extend: It is the same explicit-vs-implicit trade-off as meshes versus level sets in Chapter 8 — and note that both still depend on classical SfM to provide the camera poses.

knowledge_points.title: Single-View Density Fields, Scene Completion and Casual Video
knowledge_points.recap:
**Density fields for single-view reconstruction ("Behind the Scenes", Wimbauer et al., CVPR 2023).** A single image is lifted to a **density field** rather than a depth map. A depth map only records the first visible surface; a density field predicts occupancy **throughout** the volume, including regions **occluded** in the input view. Training is again self-supervised by **novel-view synthesis**: render the field into other frames of a video and compare photometrically, so no 3D ground truth is required.
**Self-supervised semantic scene completion.** The same idea extended with semantics — predict occupancy **and** class label for the whole volume, including unobserved parts, supervised only by multi-view photometric and semantic consistency. Benchmarks such as OccuFly evaluate this task.
**Reconstruction from casual video.** Classical SfM assumes a static scene, a calibrated camera and good parallax. Casual internet video breaks all three. Recent systems relax them:
$\bullet$ **AnyCam** — self-supervised on casual videos, predicting camera motion (and intrinsics) without ground truth poses;
$\bullet$ **Align3R** — aligning per-frame 3D predictions into a consistent reconstruction;
$\bullet$ **BA-Track** and **ViSTA-SLAM** — pairing learned two-view association with classical bundle adjustment / pose-graph optimisation (ViSTA-SLAM: "Visual SLAM with symmetric two-view association").
The recurring pattern: a **learned front end** proposes correspondences or per-frame geometry, and a **classical back end** (bundle adjustment, pose graph) enforces global consistency.
**4D and deformation.** Beyond static scenes: **4Deform** (neural surface deformation for robust shape interpolation), volume-preserving shape interpolation, and **TwoSquared** (4D generation from 2D image pairs) extend reconstruction to deforming objects and to generation with diffusion priors.

questions.q: What is a density field for single-view reconstruction, how does it differ from predicting a depth map, and how can it be trained without 3D ground truth?
questions.answer:
**Depth map.** One depth value per pixel: it records only the **first visible surface** along each ray. Everything behind that surface — and everything occluded — is simply absent from the representation.
**Density field.** A volumetric function predicting occupancy/density at **every** 3D point in the frustum, so it also represents the parts of the scene **hidden behind** the visible surface. That is what allows novel views that look "behind" objects, hence the name of the method.
**Training without 3D ground truth.** Self-supervision by **novel-view synthesis**: render the predicted density field into *other* frames of the same video (whose relative poses are known or estimated) and minimise the photometric difference with the real frames. Because occluded geometry becomes visible in those other views, the supervision signal reaches exactly the regions a depth map cannot represent — no 3D annotations are required.
questions.extend: The same self-supervised, photometric recipe as D3VO and NeRF: geometry is learned by being forced to explain other views of the same scene.

questions.q: Why does classical structure-from-motion struggle on casual video, and what is the common architectural pattern of recent systems (AnyCam, Align3R, BA-Track, ViSTA-SLAM) that address it?
questions.answer:
**Why classical SfM struggles.** It assumes a **static** scene, a **calibrated** camera and sufficient **parallax** with well-textured, matchable features. Casual video violates all of these: people and objects move, the intrinsics are unknown and may change (zoom, auto-focus), motion is often near-rotational or shaky, and clips are short with motion blur and rolling shutter.
**The common pattern.** A **learned front end** supplies what matching alone cannot — per-frame depth or point maps, dense two-view associations, motion masks, and often the intrinsics — while a **classical geometric back end** (bundle adjustment, pose-graph optimisation) enforces global consistency across the sequence. Training is typically **self-supervised** on video, again through photometric / reprojection consistency.
**Examples.** AnyCam predicts camera motion self-supervised on casual video; Align3R aligns per-frame 3D predictions into one reconstruction; ViSTA-SLAM combines symmetric two-view association with SLAM-style optimisation.
questions.extend: The lesson of the chapter: learning replaces the brittle *correspondence* stage, not the geometry — the optimisation back end from Chapters 6 and 7 survives.

knowledge_points.title: Event Cameras and Event-Based SLAM
knowledge_points.recap:
**What an event camera is.** A bio-inspired sensor (Lichtsteiner, Posch, Delbrück, 2006/2008) in which every pixel fires **asynchronously and independently** whenever the logarithmic brightness at that pixel changes by more than a threshold. The output is not a frame but a stream of **events** $(x,y,t,p)$: pixel coordinates, a microsecond timestamp, and the polarity of the change.
**Why it matters for 3D vision.**
$\bullet$ **Microsecond temporal resolution** and no motion blur — the sensor keeps working during motion that would smear a conventional frame beyond use;
$\bullet$ **Very high dynamic range** (≈120 dB vs ≈60 dB), because each pixel adapts individually — no global exposure to saturate;
$\bullet$ **Low power and low bandwidth**, since static regions emit nothing.
**Why it is hard.** Everything in this course assumes *frames* and *brightness constancy*. Events carry no absolute intensity — only changes — so feature detectors, photometric residuals and correspondence search all have to be redesigned. Events are also triggered only where there is a **gradient and motion**, so a static camera sees nothing.
**Event-based SLAM.** A line of work runs from event-based 3D SLAM with a depth-augmented dynamic vision sensor (Weikersdorfer et al., ICRA 2014) and real-time tracking and mapping with an event camera (Kim et al., ECCV 2016; EVO, Rebecq et al., 2017), through hybrid systems combining events, frames and IMU for robustness in HDR and high-speed scenarios (Ultimate SLAM), to **DEVO — Deep Event Visual Odometry**, which asks whether high-precision *monocular, event-only* visual odometry is achievable and answers it with a learned front end evaluated across seven datasets.
**Benchmarks.** The **TUM VIE** dataset provides event, frame and IMU data with motion-capture ground truth for exactly this evaluation.

questions.q: What is an event camera, what does it output, and what are its advantages and challenges for visual odometry?
questions.answer:
**What it is.** A bio-inspired sensor in which each pixel operates **independently and asynchronously**, firing whenever the **logarithmic brightness** at that pixel changes by more than a threshold.
**Output.** Not images but a stream of **events** $(x,y,t,p)$ — pixel coordinates, a microsecond-resolution timestamp, and the polarity (brightness up or down).
**Advantages.** Microsecond temporal resolution and effectively **no motion blur**, so tracking survives very fast motion; a very high **dynamic range** (~120 dB), because each pixel adapts on its own instead of sharing a global exposure; and low power / bandwidth, since static parts of the scene produce no data.
**Challenges.** There is **no absolute intensity** — only changes — so brightness constancy, conventional feature detectors and photometric residuals do not transfer directly and the whole front end must be redesigned. Events appear only where there is both a **gradient and motion**, so a stationary camera observes nothing, and the asynchronous, noisy stream needs its own representation before it can be fed to geometry or a network.
**State of the art.** Systems range from geometric event-based tracking and mapping (EVO) and hybrid event+frame+IMU pipelines (Ultimate SLAM) to **DEVO**, a deep monocular event-only visual odometry evaluated on seven datasets; the **TUM VIE** dataset provides events, frames, IMU and motion-capture ground truth for benchmarking.
questions.extend: An event camera measures the *temporal derivative* of log intensity — literally the $I_t$ term of the optical flow constraint, sampled asynchronously.
